theme: The narrow door; the great banquet; the lost sheep, coin, son
readingInstruction: Read Luke 13:22-15:32. The narrow door, a banquet where the guests make excuses, the cost of discipleship, and three parables about the lost: a sheep, a coin, and a son. Chapter 15 is among the most loved in the Bible.
settingTheScene: Jesus is still on the way to Jerusalem. Someone asks whether only a few will be saved, and Jesus replies with a warning. Then he dines with a Pharisee on the Sabbath and tells about banquets. Tax collectors and sinners draw near to hear him, and the Pharisees grumble. In response, Jesus tells three parables of lost things, and the third becomes the best known of all his stories.
observation: “Strive to enter through the narrow door” (13:24).
“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets… How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (13:34).
“For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (14:11).
“Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled” (14:23).
“Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple” (14:27).
“There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” (15:7).
“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (15:20).
“For this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found” (15:32).
interpretation:
Someone asks if only a few will be saved. Jesus does not answer with a number but with a command: strive to enter the narrow door. Many will seek to enter and not be able. The door will be shut, and those outside will say, “We ate and drank in your presence.” Being near Jesus is not the same as knowing him. Yet people will come from east, west, north, and south to sit at table in the kingdom, and “some who are last will be first.” Jesus mourns over Jerusalem like a mother hen. “You were not willing.”

At a Pharisee’s table, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, and teaches that the humble will be exalted. He tells the host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, who cannot repay. Then he tells of a great banquet where invited guests make excuses. The master sends his servants to the poor, then to the highways and hedges. “That my house may be filled.” The kingdom is a feast, and the grace of the host reaches the outcast. Jesus then warns the crowds about the cost of following him. One must count the cost, like a builder or a king. No one can be his disciple without giving up everything.

The three parables of chapter 15 answer the grumbling Pharisees. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine to find one lost sheep, carries it home on his shoulders, and calls friends to rejoice. A woman sweeps the house for one lost coin, and rejoices when it is found. In each, the lost is sought and found, and heaven rejoices.

The third story is of a father and two sons. The younger son demands his inheritance, wastes it, and ends up feeding pigs. “He came to himself.” He plans a speech and heads home. “While he was still a long way off, his father saw him,” ran, embraced him, and kissed him. He interrupts the speech, calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals, and a feast. This is how God receives a returning sinner.

But there is an older brother, who stays outside, angry. He has been dutiful, yet he does not share his father’s joy. The father goes out to him, too: “All that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate.” The story ends without telling us whether he goes in. Jesus leaves the Pharisees with the question. Will they join the feast, or stay outside?
connection: Isaiah 55:6-7 invites the wicked to return to the LORD, who will abundantly pardon. Ezekiel 34:11-16 has God as the seeking shepherd. Psalm 103:8-13 says the LORD has compassion as a father has compassion on his children. Hosea 11 shows God’s tender love for a wandering son. Matthew 7:13-14 parallels the narrow gate. Romans 5:8 says God shows his love in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Ephesians 2:13 says we who were far off have been brought near.
application:
Imagine yourself in the story as the younger son, then as the older. Which is harder to see in yourself?

Is there someone you have written off as lost? Pray for them by name.

Celebrate when someone repents or comes to faith. Heaven does.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for running to meet you while you were far off.
Tell him where you have been the older brother.
Rejoice with him over those who come home.
